blocks.x: Generation Kill is a brutally realistic miniseries set at the beginning of the Iraq War, in the opening stages of the United States' military invasion, in search of Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein. The series is based on a memoir of the same name by Evan Wright, an American war correspondent who spent a considerable length of time embedded in Iraq with an American military unit. Basically, if the show seems real, that's because much of it is — it is a dramatization of actual events, depicting actual firefights and casualties, recreated right in front of the audience. Wright himself even makes an appearance in the show, played by Lee Tergesen. However, he is only a small part of the series and isn't mentioned by name. The focus is mostly on the soldiers here.

What's cool is that one of the soldiers, Sergeant Rudy Reyes, is actually played by Reyes himself, adding even more authenticity to the situation. The show was a bold move, as the Iraq War was a bit of a sore subject in American media at the time due to public opposition, and it was still ongoing at the time of the show's release. Despite this, it was a massive success, because it allowed American audiences to see a gruesome, unsanitized version of the conflict that most media outlets were too afraid of showing. It's a masterpiece of television, and one of the finest war miniseries ever made.

blocks.c: James Badge Dale in HBO's The Pacific.

blocks.x: The second miniseries in the Band of Brothers universe, The Pacific follows an American ground infantry unit during the Second World War. The soldiers at the heart of the show are assigned to the Pacific Theater, where the enemy isn't Nazi Germany, but Imperial Japan. Following the Attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, the US began a bloody island-hopping campaign in the Pacific Islands, intent on putting a halt to the rapid expansion of Japan. Like the other miniseries in the same universe, The Pacific puts viewers right in the heart of the action through some of the bloodiest and most famous battles of the war.

Audiences will begin with the Guadalcanal Campaign in the Solomon Islands, followed by the Battle of Peleliu in present-day Palau, before concluding with the Battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, the southernmost isles of Japan itself. The difference here is that the Japanese are in their element in the thick jungles and swamps of the Pacific. Guerrilla warfare reigns supreme, often taking American forces by surprise and wreaking havoc on organized units. As with the others of its ilk, HBO's The Pacific makes sure not to pull any punches in its portrayal of combat. Expect a lot of blood and gore, true to the nature of war itself. It's not for the faint of heart, but for those who love seeing realistic portrayals of warfare, this is a superb pick.

blocks.c: band of brothers is still a masterpiece

blocks.x: Following the success of their 1998 feature film Saving Private Ryan, Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg came up with Band of Brothers, a miniseries that went on to make history. The show is very much in the spirit of Saving Private Ryan, being an unflinching, honest depiction of what World War II really looked like from the front lines. The show follows an American Airborne unit as they parachute behind enemy lines in some of the most dangerous engagements of the war's Western Front.

The show opens up with a training episode, followed by the squad's first operation, parachuting into Normandy in the wee hours of the morning on D-Day. Considering Saving Private Ryan is also set on D-Day, but is about the amphibious beach landings, Band of Brothers provided a much different perspective on things. The series continues through the Battle of Carentan before finishing off at the Battle of the Bulge, the final offensive that the Nazis made against the Allies on the Western Front, beginning in the chilly winter of December 1944. This show is just phenomenal, defining genre rules and depicting some of the greatest, most heroic moments of the war. It just doesn't get any better than this.

'The Pacific' (2010)

Image via HBO.

The second miniseries in the Band of Brothers universe, The Pacific follows an American ground infantry unit during the Second World War. The soldiers at the heart of the show are assigned to the Pacific Theater, where the enemy isn't Nazi Germany, but Imperial Japan. Following the Attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, the US began a bloody island-hopping campaign in the Pacific Islands, intent on putting a halt to the rapid expansion of Japan. Like the other miniseries in the same universe, The Pacific puts viewers right in the heart of the action through some of the bloodiest and most famous battles of the war.

Audiences will begin with the Guadalcanal Campaign in the Solomon Islands, followed by the Battle of Peleliu in present-day Palau, before concluding with the Battles of Iwo Jima and Okinawa, the southernmost isles of Japan itself. The difference here is that the Japanese are in their element in the thick jungles and swamps of the Pacific. Guerrilla warfare reigns supreme, often taking American forces by surprise and wreaking havoc on organized units. As with the others of its ilk, HBO's The Pacific makes sure not to pull any punches in its portrayal of combat. Expect a lot of blood and gore, true to the nature of war itself. It's not for the faint of heart, but for those who love seeing realistic portrayals of warfare, this is a superb pick.

'Band of Brothers' (2001)

Image via HBO

Following the success of their 1998 feature film Saving Private Ryan, Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg came up with Band of Brothers, a miniseries that went on to make history. The show is very much in the spirit of Saving Private Ryan, being an unflinching, honest depiction of what World War II really looked like from the front lines. The show follows an American Airborne unit as they parachute behind enemy lines in some of the most dangerous engagements of the war's Western Front.

The show opens up with a training episode, followed by the squad's first operation, parachuting into Normandy in the wee hours of the morning on D-Day. Considering Saving Private Ryan is also set on D-Day, but is about the amphibious beach landings, Band of Brothers provided a much different perspective on things. The series continues through the Battle of Carentan before finishing off at the Battle of the Bulge, the final offensive that the Nazis made against the Allies on the Western Front, beginning in the chilly winter of December 1944. This show is just phenomenal, defining genre rules and depicting some of the greatest, most heroic moments of the war. It just doesn't get any better than this.
